lead: A biosensor is named twice: by the biological element that recognises the target and by the transducer that turns recognition into a signal. Enzyme with an amperometric electrode gives the glucose strip; antibody with an optical surface gives the surface plasmon resonance immunosensor. The cases exams ask for are the ISFET, the IMFET and the glucose sensor.
prereq: You need chemical sensors and biosensors for the biosensor block diagram, semiconductor sensors and sensor materials for the FET as a transducer, and sensitivity, selectivity and drift from the static characteristics of sensors.

sections.h3: Two axes give every biosensor its name

blocks.text: A biosensor has two parts in series: a biological element that recognises one molecule, and a transducer that converts that recognition into a voltage, a current or a light level. Enzyme + amperometric = glucose sensor. Antibody + optical = surface plasmon resonance immunosensor. DNA + FET = GenFET.
The element sets the selectivity. Four families cover most work.

items: Enzyme: catalyses one reaction and is reusable and fast, for example glucose oxidase, urease, penicillinase.
Antibody: grips one antigen tightly; very selective but usually single-use.
DNA or aptamer: a strand pairs with its complement; an aptamer is a short folded strand that holds a small molecule.
Whole cell: a bacterium or tissue slice, for mixtures, as in BOD and toxicity tests.

blocks.text: The transducer sets the signal: electrochemical (amperometric, potentiometric or conductometric), optical, acoustic (see solid electrolyte and SAW sensors), calorimetric and FET types.

Start with an n-channel MOSFET. Remove the metal gate and leave the gate oxide bare, touching the electrolyte. That is an ISFET, an ion-sensitive field-effect transistor. A Ag/AgCl reference electrode dips into the solution and sets the gate bias: the electrolyte forms the gate, but it has no defined potential of its own.

The bare oxide carries silanol groups. Si–OH ⇌ Si–O⁻ + H⁺, and Si–OH + H⁺ ⇌ Si–OH₂⁺. At high pH the surface loses protons, becomes negative, and pushes electrons out of the channel below. The threshold voltage rises, and at a fixed gate bias the drain current falls because the overdrive V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> shrinks.

blocks.where: ΔV<sub>T</sub> is the threshold shift in volts; k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K; T is the absolute temperature in kelvin; q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. 59 mV per pH is the ideal slope at 25 °C and 61.5 mV at 37 °C. Bare SiO₂ gives only 30 to 40 mV per pH, so practical ISFETs add a silicon nitride, alumina or tantalum oxide layer that comes close to the ideal.

blocks.text: Two errors dominate: drift, as the oxide hydrates over hours, which needs frequent recalibration; and hysteresis, a reading that depends on whether the previous sample was acid or alkali.

IMFET (immunologically modified FET). An antibody or an antigen is immobilised on the gate. Binding adds charge to the surface and shifts the threshold, so the device is label-free and needs no fluorescent tag. The weakness is ionic strength: counter-ions in a salty buffer screen the bound charge within about a nanometre, so only binding right at the surface is seen.

EnFET (enzyme FET). An enzyme layer sits over the ISFET gate and the local pH change reports the substrate. Urease on urea releases ammonia and the local pH rises; penicillinase on penicillin releases acid and the local pH falls. The initial rate of pH change gives the concentration.

Glucose oxidase (GOx) is the enzyme. It carries an FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) cofactor and catalyses the reaction below. Glucose is oxidised, oxygen is the electron acceptor, and hydrogen peroxide is the product the electrode sees.
glucose + O₂ → gluconolactone + H₂O₂ (catalysed by GOx)
blocks.where: O₂ is dissolved oxygen; gluconolactone is the oxidised product; H₂O₂ is the species the electrode oxidises.

blocks.text: First generation. The H₂O₂ is oxidised at a platinum electrode held at about +0.6 to +0.7 V against Ag/AgCl. Each glucose molecule hands over two electrons, so the current is proportional to the glucose reaching the enzyme. The flaw is the high potential: ascorbic acid, uric acid and paracetamol in blood also oxidise near +0.7 V and add a false current.
Q = n<sub>e</sub> F,  I = Q / t
blocks.where: Q is charge in coulombs; n<sub>e</sub> is the moles of electrons, twice the moles of glucose; F = 96 485 C/mol; I is the average current in amperes over t seconds.

blocks.text: Second generation. A mediator such as ferrocene or ferricyanide carries electrons from the enzyme's FAD to the electrode, so the electrode can run at about +0.2 to +0.4 V. Fewer interferents oxidise there, and dissolved oxygen no longer limits the reaction. Third-generation sensors aim at direct electron transfer from the enzyme to the electrode with no mediator at all.

items: Disposable strip: a finger-prick drop (under 1 µL now, 5 to 10 µL in older strips) fills a capillary, a fixed potential is applied for about 5 s, and the current gives the glucose.
Continuous monitor: a fine needle in interstitial fluid reports every few minutes for days.

blocks.text: Normal fasting blood glucose is about 3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L, that is 70 to 100 mg/dL using 1 mmol/L = 18 mg/dL. A fasting value of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more on repeat tests points to diabetes, so a meter must read well across 2 to 30 mmol/L; diagnosis rules belong to a medical text.

examples.question: An older disposable glucose strip is filled with 10 µL of blood whose glucose concentration is 5.5 mmol/L. Each glucose molecule releases 2 electrons at the platinum electrode. The enzyme reaction goes to completion in 10 s. Find (a) the moles of glucose, (b) the moles of electrons, (c) the total charge and (d) the average current. Take F = 96 485 C/mol.
steps: Convert the volume to litres: 10 µL = 10 × 10⁻⁶ L = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ L.
Moles of glucose: n<sub>g</sub> = c × V = 5.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L × 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ L = 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ mol.
Moles of electrons: n<sub>e</sub> = 2 × n<sub>g</sub> = 2 × 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ mol.
Charge: Q = n<sub>e</sub> × F = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ mol × 96 485 C/mol = 1.061 × 10⁻² C = 10.6 mC.
Average current: I = Q / t = 1.061 × 10⁻² C / 10 s = 1.061 × 10⁻³ A = 1.06 mA.
This is an upper bound: a real strip reacts only the glucose near the electrode in a few seconds, so its current is a few microamperes.
examples.answer: The strip would pass 10.6 mC, an average of about 1.06 mA over the 10 s, if all the glucose reacted; real strips react only a fraction and pass microamperes.

examples.question: A blood-gas analyser uses an ISFET with a silicon nitride gate at 37 °C. Its slope is 90 % of the ideal Nernstian value. (a) Find the ideal slope at 37 °C. (b) Find the device slope. (c) A patient's blood pH falls from 7.40 to 7.30. Find the threshold shift and its direction. (d) Find the voltage resolution the readout needs to show 0.01 pH.
steps: (c) ΔpH = 7.30 − 7.40 = −0.10, so ΔV<sub>T</sub> = 55.4 × (−0.10) = −5.54 mV. More H⁺ makes the surface more positive, so the threshold falls by 5.5 mV and, at fixed gate bias, the drain current rises.
(d) 0.01 pH × 55.4 mV per pH = 0.554 mV, so the readout must resolve about 0.5 mV and the device drift over a run must stay well below that.
Check: a 0.10 pH fall is a large change in blood, yet it is only 5.5 mV, so the reference electrode and the temperature must be held steady.
examples.answer: The ideal slope at 37 °C is 61.5 mV/pH and the device gives 55.4 mV/pH; a pH fall from 7.40 to 7.30 lowers the threshold by 5.54 mV; the readout needs about 0.55 mV resolution for 0.01 pH.

traps: Reversing the ISFET sign. For an n-channel device at a fixed gate bias the output falls as pH rises, because the threshold voltage rises and the overdrive shrinks.
Forgetting the 2 electrons per glucose molecule, or using the moles of glucose directly in Q = nF. The factor of two comes from H₂O₂ oxidation at platinum.
Calling a bare ISFET a biosensor. It is a pH sensor until an enzyme or antibody layer makes it an EnFET or an IMFET.

quiz.q: What physical change turns a MOSFET into an ISFET?
quiz.a: The metal gate is removed and the gate oxide is left exposed to the electrolyte; a reference electrode supplies the gate bias.

quiz.q: Why does an ISFET need a reference electrode when the solution already touches the gate oxide?
quiz.a: A liquid has no fixed potential of its own. The Ag/AgCl reference closes the circuit and defines the gate-to-source voltage, so a pH reading means something and can be repeated.

quiz.q: An n-channel ISFET at 25 °C reads pH 7.00 and then pH 7.40. Using 59 mV/pH, find the change in threshold voltage and state the direction of the current change.
quiz.a: ΔV<sub>T</sub> = 59 mV/pH × 0.40 pH = 23.6 mV. The threshold rises, so at fixed gate bias the drain current falls.

quiz.q: An IMFET gives a strong signal in dilute buffer but almost none in a high-salt buffer at the same antigen concentration. Explain.
quiz.a: Ionic screening. Counter-ions in the electrolyte shield the charge of the bound antigen within about a nanometre, the Debye length, so the gate never feels the binding charge. Lowering the ionic strength widens the screening length and the signal returns.

quiz.q: Why does a ferrocene mediator reduce interference in a glucose sensor?
quiz.a: Ferrocene carries electrons from the enzyme's FAD to the electrode at about +0.2 to +0.4 V. Hydrogen peroxide needs +0.6 to +0.7 V. Ascorbate, urate and paracetamol oxidise at the higher potential, so running lower removes most of their false current. The mediator also removes the dependence on dissolved oxygen.

beyond: Not for the exam. Microneedle patches read interstitial glucose without a finger prick, and continuous monitors are being closed into a loop with insulin pumps. Search Debye length in FET biosensors and aptamer FET sensors.
